newsitem.title: FRANCE: Prodi warns of turmoil if lira excluded from euro.
newsitem.headline: Prodi warns of turmoil if lira excluded from euro.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi warned on Monday that if the lira were left out of a single European currency in 1999 the reaction in financial markets would be impossible to control.

Asked whether Italy would obstruct the entry of Spain and Portugal if Italy were left out of the euro-club, Prodi said "Italy is determined to use all political instruments at its disposal" to ensure the lira joins the planned single currency.

Prodi told French business daily La Tribune the efficiency of any exchange rate mechanism, or ERM II, put in place when the euro is launched in 1999, would depend on an environment of co-operation and solidarity between member states.
"No ERM II will prevent the fact that events will be impossible to control if the lira is not in the euro," Prodi said.

"But what solidarity is conceivable in the case of a fight?," Prodi asked. "In the event of a negative decision against Italy on the euro, the context would be more one of hostility than co-operation."

Prodi said he did not rule out a political crisis in Europe over the issue. "I hope there won't be one... We well understand the interests of our partners, but we also have own interests which we are determined to defend."
Italy has taken drastic action to try and slash its deficit enough in 1997 to qualify for membership of the single currency but Rome's European Union partners cast doubt on its efforts on Monday.

EU finance ministers meeting in Brussels on Monday approved a sharply worded report on the state of Italy's finances, suggesting that many of the measures taken to cut the budget deficit were not sustainable.
By contrast both Spain and Portugal received praise for their efforts to catch up with the European Union's northern economies.

Prodi reiterated in the interview that Italy would meet the strict three percent target for its public deficit as a percentage of gross domestic product in 1997 and pledged to keep Italy's finances stable in the future through a combination of exceptional and structural measures.

Meanwhile Gaullist French National Assembly President Philippe Seguin, a possible successor to Prime Minister Alain Juppe, threw his weight on Monday behind Italy's claims to membership for what he said was the good of Europe as a whole.

Seguin said in a television interview, "We need the presence of Italy, first of all for reasons of equilibrium within Europe. If Italy didn't enter, we would have by definition a lira that would devalue and a very big unemployment problem."
